extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students concerned with drafting and litigating patent specifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for what a patent specification must contain and how it will be judged (enablement, sufficiency, drawings, signatures, amendments, and claim-construction issues). Focused on enabling a workman of ordinary skill and on formal/statutory requisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, open, and candid exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the honest, open, and candid exposition by the patentee of everything that is necessary for the easy and certain procurement of that for which the patent is granted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must disclose all that is necessary so others can practice the invention; whether disclosure suffices is a question of fact for a jury upon evidence of persons skilled in the art (example: brick clay proportions dispute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must clearly and fully describe the invention and give the best known process/materials/methods
rubrics_metrics.description: 'it is necessary that a specification should clearly and fully describe the invention, and should give the best process, material, and methods known to the inventor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee should set out the best mode known; but the specification need not detail operations or materials that are within ordinary knowledge of workmen, nor recount known processes or explain technical terms familiar to the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — enable a workman of ordinary skill to make the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must be such 'as to enable a workman of ordinary skill' to make the machine or compound described; if a competent workman could not make it from the specification, the patent may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether competent witnesses can produce the result from the specification. If the specification, read as a whole, enables the skilled operator to practice the invention, minor ambiguities will not defeat it. Examples include alloy and photographic-process cases discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No material untrue statements that would mislead a competent workman
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification contains an untrue statement in a material circumstance 'of such a nature that, if literally acted upon by a competent workman, it would mislead him, and cause the experiment to fail, the specification is therefore bad, and the patent invalidated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a skilled workman could correct the error in practice, a materially false statement that would mislead if followed literally can invalidate the patent. However, courts will not apply this rule too rigidly for slight or grammatical obscurities in lengthy processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of ranges/proportions must be truthful and operative at extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee gives certain limits or proportions (e.g., ranges of alloy composition or mixture proportions), if particular specified extremes would not perform as claimed, that falsity may invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat the accuracy of claimed ranges as a question of fact for the jury. If the patentee asserts that 'both of which extremes, and all intermediate proportions, will' produce a property, but evidence shows some extremes fail, the patent may be defeated (example: copper/zinc proportion disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: If a particular material is essential, the specification must direct its use
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is not necessary... to state of what material every part should be made, where the principle of operation and the effect are the same... but, if a particular material be essential to the successful operation of the machine, as the patentee uses it, he must direct the use of that material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit essential material limitations. If success depends on a specific material, the specification must identify and instruct use of that material; general statements that principle works across materials suffice only if true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for operative discretion and imprecise language where skill supplies detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'a little below the point of fusion' indicate the degree 'which, in the hands of an operator of skill and judgment, would effect practically and successfully the object of his invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court accepts language that leaves reasonable discretion to skilled operators; providing a fixed physical referent (e.g., melting point) or language that implies expert judgment is ordinarily sufficient. Such latitude does not render a specification uncertain if it still gives a 'fixed rule' that can be safely followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositions with approximate proportions can be sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions stating approximate proportions (e.g., 'about from four ounces to a pound of sulphur to a pound of rubber') are sufficient if properly reduced to practice will produce the claimed article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive direction may be exhausted by giving the proportions and process; remaining work is that of a skilled workman. If, however, the described proportions fail to produce the article when properly practiced, then validity is a different question (may require experiment to determine optimum proportion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings required when nature of the case admits and form part of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: For machinery the statute directs annexing 'a drawing or drawings, and written references, where the nature of the case admits of drawings.' Drawings 'constitute a part of the specification' when annexed and may be used to explain or help out an otherwise imperfect written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and drawings are to be examined together; drawings may correct or explain ambiguities in the text. References from writing to drawing are required only where necessary for understanding; drawings need not be explicitly mentioned in the specification if on file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings need not be to scale but must be sufficient to enable practice
rubrics_metrics.description: It was once thought drawings must be on scale, but now if a mechanic can make the subject from a perspective drawing, scale is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject could not be made without many experiments unless the drawing is to scale, then the combined specification (writing + drawing) would be defective. Thus use the scale only when necessary to avoid undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures and attestations required by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires a formal attestation: 'they must be signed by the inventor and by two witnesses.' (Act of 1870: 'the specification and claim shall be signed by the inventor, and attested by two witnesses').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper execution and witness attestations; a copy of the drawings shall be attached to the patent as part of the specification. There is some historical ambiguity whether drawings must be separately signed, but current statutory language requires signature and attestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent improvements cannot be annexed to issued patent (modern rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of 1836 allowed annexing descriptions of improvements after issuance, but the act of 1861 repealed that provision; 'in all cases where additional improvements would now be admissible, independent patents must be applied for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-issuance improvements should be the subject of new patent applications; improvements entered before repeal remain valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested substitutions and equivalence are construed by specification proportions and are fact questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specification suggests substitution of one component for another (e.g., 'naphtha' for 'kerosene') but prescribes proportions, the substitution is construed in light of those proportions; whether one compound is 'substantially the same' as another differing in proportions is a question of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims using suggested substitutions will be interpreted according to the proportions expressly prescribed; expert evidence may be required to determine substantial equivalence (example: Tyler v. Boston, naphtha/kerosene proportions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor dimensional deviations that a workman of ordinary skill would make are acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: A deviation from precise dimensions shown so as to make different parts work together 'is within the knowledge of any workman.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a model copied exactly from drawings 'would not work' because one part is slightly too small, an ordinary skilled workman is expected to recognize and correct such defects; specification is sufficient if it enables such common-sense adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scientific/technical terms addressed to skilled persons is permissible but common language must not mislead the ordinary man
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A specification containing scientific terms, which are not understood, except by persons acquainted with the nature of the business, is not bad because an ordinary person does not understand it... but a specification using common language, and stating that by which a common man may be misled... would not be good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor wording to the audience of skilled operators in the art; avoid common-language formulations that create a false impression for ordinary readers when the specification does not intend such a meaning.
